md_description: This DAG represents a human-subject EEG experiment in which visual stimuli are presented while brain electrical activity is recorded to extract event-related potentials. It includes subject preparation, stimulus timing definition, EEG acquisition, behavioral response capture, preprocessing, epoching, ERP derivation, and joint analysis of neural and response measures.

human_subject.reasoning: For the human_subject Entity node, I included only intrinsic participant metadata that exists before any preparation or recording: identifiers, basic demographics, handedness, vision status, and relevant eligibility/origin fields. I excluded anything that belongs to downstream preparation, capture, signal, or derivative nodes, such as cap fit, EEG settings, stimulus exposure, responses, file properties, preprocessing, epochs, or ERP results. I also avoided repeating experiment-wide IDs if those were already generated elsewhere; since no already_generated fields were provided here, I kept the schema focused on unique subject-level descriptors needed to identify the participant and interpret EEG/ERP data.

md_schema.descr: Unique participant identifier for the enrolled human subject in this EEG ERP study; use a stable string such as 'sub-001'. Assigned at enrollment and used to link all subject-derived data without revealing personal identity.

Biological sex recorded at enrollment for the participant, as reported or extracted from study records. Useful for cohort description and potential EEG/ERP subgroup analysis; allowed values should match the study form.
Participant age in years at the time of enrollment or first EEG session. Typical adult human-subject range for this workflow is about 18 to 65 years; record as an integer.
Participant handedness recorded at enrollment, because lateralization can matter for EEG/ERP interpretation. Use the study’s categorical hand-preference classification.
Participant visual status at enrollment, relevant because the experiment presents visual stimuli. Record whether vision is normal or corrected-to-normal, or whether a visual impairment is present.
Whether the participant uses vision correction during the experiment, such as glasses or contact lenses. Record at enrollment because it can affect stimulus visibility.

Self-reported language proficiency relevant to task instructions, recorded at enrollment if the experiment requires understanding verbal instructions. Use a categorical study-defined level or language group.

Whether the participant reports prior neurological disease, seizure history, or other major neurological conditions at screening/enrollment. This is a subject-level eligibility descriptor, not a recording outcome.
Medication or substance status at enrollment that could affect EEG or cognition, such as sedatives or stimulant use. Record as a subject-level screening descriptor, not as a process parameter.

eeg_cap_setup.reasoning: For the eeg_cap_setup Process node, I included only setup/protocol fields that describe how the EEG cap was prepared and contact was established on the participant. This includes cap placement details, gel/paste use, montage/reference approach, impedance targets, and setup completion quality. I excluded subject identity and intrinsic participant properties because those belong to the human_subject Entity node. I also excluded instrument hardware manufacturer/model/serial details here because the Capture node owns the recording system description, and I avoided any output-file or signal-quality fields because those belong downstream to the recording signal. No already_generated fields were provided, so I did not need to suppress overlaps beyond the node-territory rules.

md_schema.descr: Type or brand family of EEG cap fitted to the participant during setup, recorded at the moment of preparation before recording begins. Example values may include size-specific caps or study-standard cap styles.
Physical size of the EEG cap used during fitting, recorded during setup to document electrode fit. Use the study’s size class or numeric sizing convention if available.
Number of electrodes present on the cap at the end of preparation, measured during setup after fitting and before acquisition. Typical EEG systems use 32, 64, 128, or similar channel counts.
Named montage or spatial layout used when placing the EEG cap, recorded during setup. Examples include standard systems such as 10-20 or 10-10 layouts.

Reference scheme configured during cap setup, describing how recording reference points are assigned before acquisition. Record the scheme used for this study, such as common average or linked mastoids.
Anatomical or cap position of the ground electrode established during setup, recorded before recording starts. Use the site name or study-specific placement label.
Whether conductive gel or paste was applied during cap preparation to improve scalp-electrode contact. Record as true if gel was used at any electrode location in the setup step.
Type of conductive material used during EEG cap setup, recorded if gel or paste was applied. Examples include saline gel, conductive paste, or hydrogel.

Maximum electrode-skin impedance target in kilo-ohms that the operator aimed to achieve during setup before recording. Typical EEG preparation targets are often below 5–20 kOhm depending on equipment and study standards.
Measured electrode-skin impedance in kilo-ohms at the end of cap preparation, recorded immediately before EEG recording begins. Use the value obtained during the final quality check of the setup.
Outcome of the cap preparation step, indicating whether the EEG cap was successfully fitted and contact quality was acceptable for recording. Record at the end of the setup process.

prepared_subject.reasoning: For the prepared_subject Entity node, I included only the participant’s post-setup readiness state: what changed after cap preparation and before any recording begins. These fields describe readiness for EEG recording and task performance, such as preparedness status, comfort, tolerance of the cap, and whether the participant is ready for stimulus presentation and response capture. I excluded cap details, gel, montage, impedance, and operator actions because those belong to the eeg_cap_setup Process node. I also excluded recording settings, stimulus timing, response-task design, and all signal/derivative properties because those belong downstream to Capture, Derivative, or Signal nodes. No already_generated list was provided, so I avoided only semantic overlap with the subject and setup nodes.

md_schema.descr: Whether the participant is ready to begin EEG acquisition after cap setup is completed. Record at the transition from preparation to recording, immediately before the first stimulus or response trial.
Whether the participant can safely and comfortably proceed to the visual-stimulus portion of the experiment. This is a post-setup readiness flag assessed before stimulus onset.
Whether the participant can perform the required behavioral response task during the upcoming recording session. Record immediately before task start, after confirming the response device is usable.
Participant-reported comfort with the EEG cap after setup, assessed before recording starts. Use the study’s ordinal or categorical comfort rating if collected.
Whether visible skin irritation or discomfort was noted after cap preparation and before recording. Record as a readiness-related subject condition, not as a setup procedure detail.
Whether the participant was informed about and agreed to remain relatively still during EEG recording. Record at readiness confirmation before task initiation.
Whether the participant demonstrated understanding of the upcoming visual-stimulus and response instructions after preparation. Record this just before starting the recording session.

stimulus_protocol.reasoning: For the stimulus_protocol Derivative node, I included only the computed/defined presentation schedule that specifies how the visual stimuli are structured across trials. These fields capture timing logic, trial sequencing, stimulus duration and inter-stimulus interval structure, condition mapping, and any counterbalancing rules needed to reproduce the protocol. I excluded the actual stimulus identities and descriptive content because those belong to the visual_stimulus_set node. I also excluded recording/capture settings, subject readiness, response-device behavior, and downstream EEG/ERP outputs because those are owned by other node types. No already_generated fields were provided, so I avoided only semantic overlap with upstream and downstream nodes while keeping the schema focused on the stimulus schedule itself.

md_schema.descr: Name or short identifier of the visual stimulus timing protocol used in this experiment, recorded for the derived schedule. Use a stable string such as 'oddball_v2' or 'blocked_faces_01'.
Total number of stimulus trials specified by the protocol, measured across the full run or block set. This is the count used to drive the presentation schedule.
Number of distinct stimulus conditions represented in the protocol, determined by the trial design before data collection begins.

Duration in milliseconds that each visual stimulus is displayed on screen during a trial, as defined by the protocol. Typical ERP experiments use durations from a few tens to a few hundred milliseconds.
Inter-stimulus interval duration in milliseconds defined by the protocol between consecutive stimulus presentations or trial events. Record the nominal schedule value used for timing.
Amount of randomized timing jitter in milliseconds applied to stimulus onset times, if the protocol includes temporal jitter. Record the nominal jitter range or step used in the derived schedule.
How trials are organized in the protocol, such as a single continuous run or multiple blocks with rest breaks. Record the schedule structure used to present stimuli.

Counterbalancing rule used in the derived stimulus schedule to distribute condition order, positions, or trial sequences across the experiment. Record the study-defined scheme applied before presentation.
Whether the order of stimulus trials is fixed by design rather than randomized at run time. Record this property of the protocol schedule, not the actual observed order.
Baseline period in milliseconds before each stimulus onset that is reserved in the timing protocol for pre-stimulus referencing or fixation. Use the nominal interval value specified by the protocol.
Duration in milliseconds after stimulus onset during which responses are expected or accepted according to the protocol. Record the task-defined response window used for timing alignment.

Study-defined mapping from protocol condition labels to experimental codes used in the timing schedule, such as mapping a condition name to an event code or label. Use a stable string representation if stored in flat metadata.

visual_stimulus_set.reasoning: I corrected the schema by removing the colliding field condition_count, which had already been generated for an earlier DAG step. I kept only stimulus-set content fields that remain specific to the visual_stimulus_set node and do not duplicate stimulus timing, capture, or subject metadata. The remaining fields describe the identity, composition, modality, and labeling structure of the visual stimulus collection needed to interpret the experiment design.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the visual stimulus set used in the experiment, recorded as the design-level label for the collection of stimuli. Use a stable string such as 'faces_vs_scenes_set_a'.
Total number of distinct visual stimulus items in the set, counted before presentation begins. This field describes the size of the stimulus library used by the protocol.
List or encoded description of the condition labels assigned to the stimuli in this set, such as category names or experimental classes. Store the labels as a flat string representation if needed.
Sensory modality of the experimental stimuli; for this node the modality should reflect visual presentation content rather than timing or acquisition parameters.
Coarse complexity level of the visual stimulus set, describing whether stimuli are simple patterns, natural images, or mixed-content items. Record as a study-defined categorical descriptor.
Color representation of the visual stimuli, recorded as a design property of the stimulus set. Examples include grayscale or full-color presentations.

Nominal visual size of stimuli in degrees of visual angle, as defined by the stimulus set or display design. Use the value that characterizes the presented stimulus image extent, typically in the range of a few degrees for ERP studies.
Background context used behind the stimuli, such as uniform blank, patterned, or task-specific backgrounds. Record the visual background property that is part of the stimulus set definition.

Rule used to assign labels to the visual stimuli, such as category-based, identity-based, or condition-based labeling. This is part of the dataset definition for the stimulus set, not the trial timing.

response_protocol.reasoning: For the response_protocol Derivative node, I included only the design of the behavioral response task: how participants are expected to respond, what response options or mappings are used, what device class the task assumes, and how response trials are structured. I excluded EEG/cap fields, subject readiness, and raw response data because those belong to Capture or Signal nodes. I also avoided reusing condition_count due to the earlier collision note, and I did not include any stimulus timing fields because those belong to stimulus_protocol. The result focuses on the task definition needed to reproduce the response collection logic.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the response task protocol used in this experiment, recorded as the design-level label for the behavioral response collection scheme. Use a stable string such as 'two_choice_button_task'.
Modality of the participant response expected by the protocol, such as button press or key press. Record the design choice used to collect behavioral responses during the EEG session.
Type of response device assumed by the protocol, such as a button box or keyboard. This describes the task design for response collection, not the captured data stream.

Mapping from response options to physical buttons or keys, defined by the protocol before data collection. Store the study-defined mapping as a flat string if needed, for example 'left=odd right=even'.
Set of permitted behavioral choices specified by the protocol, such as left/right, yes/no, or multiple forced-choice options. Record the option set used for trial responses.
Maximum time in milliseconds after stimulus onset within which a response is considered valid according to the protocol. Record the task-defined response deadline used for behavioral collection.
Start time in milliseconds relative to stimulus onset at which a response window opens, if the protocol uses delayed responding or separate cueing. Use the nominal timing defined for the task.

End time in milliseconds relative to stimulus onset at which the response window closes, if the protocol defines an explicit interval. This is part of the task design, not the captured response signal.
Whether participant feedback is enabled after a response according to the protocol. Record this task-design property at the response protocol level.
Fraction or proportion of trials reserved as catch or attention-check trials in the response protocol, if applicable. Use the nominal study design value.
Requirement for whether every trial demands a response, only some conditions demand a response, or responses are optional. Record the protocol-level response rule as a categorical design choice.

eeg_recording.reasoning: For the eeg_recording Capture node, I included only the measurement-session and instrument-configuration fields that are actively set for EEG acquisition: amplifier and acquisition software identity, sampling settings, channel configuration, recording reference/ground, filters applied during acquisition, impedance threshold, and recording start/stop state. I excluded subject properties, cap preparation details, stimulus timing, response design, and raw file properties because those belong to upstream Entity/Process nodes, downstream Signal nodes, or separate behavioral nodes. I also respected the earlier collision note by avoiding any field names already used elsewhere, including condition_count and other non-recording concepts. The schema is focused on what the operator/instrument configures at the moment of EEG capture.

md_schema.descr: Manufacturer of the EEG amplifier used for the recording session, recorded for the active capture hardware configuration. Example: a commercial EEG system vendor name.
Model name or number of the EEG amplifier used during recording. Record the specific instrument model configured for the session.
Serial number of the EEG amplifier used in the capture session, recorded to identify the specific hardware unit. Use the manufacturer-assigned string exactly as labeled on the device.

Name of the EEG acquisition software controlling data capture, recorded as part of the recording-session configuration. Example names may include vendor acquisition suites or custom recording applications.
Version of the acquisition software used during EEG recording, recorded at the time of capture. Use the exact software version string shown by the application.
Sampling rate in hertz used to digitize scalp electrical activity during the recording session. Typical EEG values are often 250, 500, 1000, or higher depending on the system.
Number of EEG channels actively recorded during the session, measured as the configured capture channel set. Typical values include 32, 64, 128, or similar.
Reference configuration applied during EEG capture, such as common average or a mastoid reference. This is the active recording setting, not the cap placement itself.
Ground configuration used by the EEG amplifier during recording, described as the active acquisition ground arrangement. Record the configured ground scheme used during the session.
Low-cut filter frequency in hertz applied online during acquisition, if any. Record the value set on the recording system at capture time.
High-cut filter frequency in hertz applied online during acquisition, if any. Record the value set on the recording system at capture time.
Notch filter frequency in hertz applied online during acquisition to suppress line noise, if used. Typical values are 50 or 60 Hz depending on the local mains frequency.

Maximum acceptable electrode impedance in kilo-ohms configured for the recording session before acquisition proceeds. Typical operational limits are often between 5 and 20 kOhm depending on the system and study standards.
Operational status of the EEG capture session, indicating whether acquisition is running, paused, or completed. Record this at the capture node as the session state.

raw_eeg_signal.reasoning: For the raw_eeg_signal Signal node, I included only file-level and raw data artefact properties: format, size, dimensions/channel counts, sampling metadata as stored in the raw signal, and basic technical quality or storage-location information. I excluded capture configuration such as amplifier model, sampling rate settings, filters, and impedance limits because those belong to the eeg_recording Capture node. I also excluded preprocessing, epochs, and ERP-derived quantities because they belong to downstream Process or Derivative nodes. No already_generated list was provided here, but I still avoided duplicate semantics by keeping the schema strictly to raw artifact characteristics.

md_schema.descr: Name of the raw EEG data file as stored after the recording session. Use the exact filename or archive item label, such as 'sub-001_run-01.edf'.
Technical file format of the raw EEG signal artifact, recorded for the stored time series. Examples include EDF, BDF, BrainVision, FIF, or other raw EEG container formats.
File size in bytes of the raw EEG signal artifact, measured from the stored data object after acquisition. Use the exact storage size for the raw file.
Number of channels present in the raw EEG time series file, counted in the stored artifact. This should reflect the raw data dimensions rather than acquisition hardware configuration.
Total number of time samples stored in the raw EEG signal artifact. Record the full sample count contained in the raw file before preprocessing or epoching.
Duration in seconds of the raw EEG time series represented by the file, measured from the stored artifact. Use the actual time span encoded in the raw recording.
Sampling rate in hertz encoded in the raw EEG file metadata. Record the stored sampling rate value as represented in the raw artifact, not the acquisition configuration field.
Time unit used in the raw EEG file representation, such as seconds or milliseconds. Record the unit in which sample times are stored or indexed.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the raw EEG signal is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the artifact location.
Technical completeness flag indicating whether the raw EEG file appears intact and fully written after acquisition. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the raw artifact.
Approximate fraction of the raw signal artifact flagged as technically problematic or missing at the file level, if assessed before preprocessing. Use a proportion between 0 and 1.
Version or revision of the raw EEG file format or writer used to encode the artifact, when available. Record the stored format version string if the container supports one.

response_capture.reasoning: For the response_capture Capture node, I included only the measurement-session and instrument-configuration fields for the behavioral response system: device manufacturer/model/serial, acquisition software, sampling or polling settings, mapped button count, and active capture state. I excluded the response protocol design itself, the participant’s actual presses or reaction times, and all EEG-related settings because those belong to the response_protocol derivative, the response_signal artifact, or the eeg_recording capture node. I also avoided repeating any field names or meanings already used for the EEG capture node, while keeping this node focused on how the response interface was configured during collection.

md_schema.descr: Manufacturer of the behavioral response device used during the task, recorded as part of the capture-system configuration. Example: vendor name of a button box or response pad.
Model name or number of the response device used during the session. Record the exact hardware model configured for behavioral capture.
Serial number of the response device used for the experiment, recorded to identify the specific hardware unit. Use the manufacturer-assigned serial string if available.
Name of the software or interface that logged behavioral responses during the experiment. Record the active capture application used with the response device.
Version of the behavioral response acquisition software used during the session. Use the exact version string visible in the recording application or log.

Polling or sampling rate in hertz used to acquire or timestamp behavioral responses. Typical values depend on the hardware/software interface and may range from low-frequency polling to high-precision timestamping.
Number of physical buttons or active response inputs configured on the device during capture. Record the device layout used to collect responses in this session.
How the response device inputs are mapped by the capture system, such as direct button-to-code mapping or software-defined remapping. Record the active mapping mode used during collection.
Operational status of the response recording session, indicating whether capture is running, paused, completed, or aborted. Record the live state of the behavioral capture interface.

Reference used to time-stamp behavioral responses during capture, such as system clock, hardware clock, or synchronized experiment clock. Record the timestamp origin configured for the response recording session.

Estimated end-to-end latency in milliseconds between physical response and recorded timestamp, if measured for the capture setup. Use the session-specific technical delay estimate for behavioral acquisition.

response_signal.reasoning: For the response_signal Signal node, I included only raw artifact properties of the behavioral response stream: file/stream format, size, number of events or rows, timestamp span, storage location, and basic technical completeness. I excluded response device configuration and timing-origin settings because those belong to the response_capture Capture node. I also excluded any summarized accuracy or reaction time metrics because those are derived behavioral analyses, not raw signal properties. The schema is limited to the stored response artefact itself so downstream users can locate, inspect, and reuse it.

md_schema.descr: Name of the raw behavioral response file or event stream artifact as stored after collection. Use the exact filename or stream label, such as 'sub-001_responses.tsv'.
Technical file format of the raw response artifact, recorded for the stored response timestamps and choices. Examples include TSV, CSV, JSON, TXT, or other event-log formats.
File size in bytes of the raw behavioral response artifact, measured from the stored data object after acquisition. Use the exact storage size for the response file.
Number of response events or rows contained in the raw response artifact. Record the total count of timestamped response entries stored in the file.
Start time in milliseconds for the raw response stream relative to the experiment or session clock. Use the first timestamp recorded in the artifact.
End time in milliseconds for the raw response stream relative to the experiment or session clock. Use the last timestamp recorded in the artifact.
Time unit used in the raw behavioral response artifact, such as milliseconds or seconds. Record the unit used to encode timestamps in the stored file.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the raw response artifact is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the response signal location.
Technical completeness flag indicating whether the raw response file appears intact and fully written after collection. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the response artifact.
Coding scheme used in the raw response artifact to represent choices, such as numeric codes, key labels, or text labels. Record the stored encoding of the raw signal, not the protocol mapping.
Approximate fraction of trials or events with missing response entries in the raw response artifact. Use a proportion between 0 and 1 if assessed at the signal file level.

eeg_preprocess.reasoning: I am correcting the eeg_preprocess Process schema to remove the colliding field notch_filter_hz, which was already generated for an earlier DAG step. I kept only preprocessing-specific fields that remain within the transformation territory of this node: software identity, filtering choices other than the removed field, artifact-cleaning strategy, bad-channel handling, re-referencing, and output quality. I excluded raw/capture properties and downstream cleaned-signal properties as before, and I avoided any repeated semantic overlap with fields already generated elsewhere.

md_schema.descr: Name of the preprocessing software or library used to transform the raw EEG signal. Example: 'MNE-Python', 'EEGLAB', or another analysis package used for cleaning.
Version of the preprocessing software used for EEG cleaning and filtering. Record the exact version string active when the preprocessing step was run.
Repository or distribution source for the preprocessing software, if relevant to reproducibility. Use a stable URL or package source string when available.
High-pass filter cutoff in hertz applied during preprocessing to remove slow drift from the raw EEG signal. Typical values are often in the 0.1 to 1 Hz range for ERP workflows.

Low-pass filter cutoff in hertz applied during preprocessing to limit high-frequency noise in the raw EEG signal. Typical ERP preprocessing uses values around 20 to 40 Hz or study-specific alternatives.
Method used to detect and remove or mark EEG artifacts during preprocessing, such as thresholding, ICA-based cleaning, or automated rejection rules.
Amplitude threshold in microvolts used for artifact rejection during preprocessing, if threshold-based cleaning is applied. Record the cutoff used on the raw EEG.
Number of independent components estimated during ICA-based artifact cleaning, if ICA was used in preprocessing. Record the component count chosen for decomposition.
Number of channels marked as bad during preprocessing before interpolation or exclusion. Record the count after cleaning decisions are applied.
Action taken on channels marked as bad during preprocessing, such as interpolation, exclusion, or retention. This describes the cleaning operation applied to the raw data.
Re-referencing method applied during preprocessing, if any, such as average reference or mastoid reference. Record the transformation applied to the raw EEG before event alignment.

Overall technical quality indicator for the cleaned EEG output after preprocessing, such as whether the data are suitable for epoching and ERP analysis. Record the preprocessing outcome at the end of the step.

clean_eeg_signal.reasoning: For the clean_eeg_signal Signal node, I included only the properties of the processed EEG artifact itself: file name/format, size, channel and sample dimensions, duration, storage location, and technical quality/completeness metrics. I excluded the preprocessing method, filter settings, ICA parameters, and re-referencing choices because those belong to the eeg_preprocess Process node. I also avoided any stimulus-locked epoch or ERP summaries because those belong downstream to epoch_extraction and erp_averaging. Because the earlier collision note flagged notch_filter_hz as already used, I did not reuse that field name or its meaning here. The schema stays focused on the stored cleaned signal as a reusable data artifact.

md_schema.descr: Name of the cleaned EEG data file as stored after preprocessing. Use the exact filename or archive label, such as 'sub-001_run-01_clean.fif'.
Technical file format of the cleaned EEG signal artifact, recorded for the processed time series. Examples include FIF, EDF, BrainVision, BDF, NWB, or other cleaned EEG containers.
File size in bytes of the cleaned EEG signal artifact, measured from the stored processed data object. Use the exact storage size after preprocessing.
Number of channels present in the cleaned EEG time series file, counted in the stored processed artifact. This reflects the post-cleaning data dimensions.
Total number of time samples stored in the cleaned EEG signal artifact. Record the full sample count available after preprocessing and artifact reduction.
Duration in seconds of the cleaned EEG time series represented by the file, measured from the stored processed artifact. Use the actual encoded time span.
Sampling rate in hertz encoded in the cleaned EEG file metadata. Record the stored sampling rate value for the processed artifact.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the cleaned EEG signal is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the processed artifact location.
Technical completeness flag indicating whether the cleaned EEG file appears intact and fully written after preprocessing. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the cleaned artifact.
Approximate fraction of the cleaned EEG artifact removed, interpolated, or otherwise altered during preprocessing, if available at the signal-file level. Use a proportion between 0 and 1.
Data type of the stored cleaned EEG samples, such as float32 or int16, if the file metadata exposes it. Record the numeric representation used in the artifact.
Version or revision of the cleaned EEG file format or writer used to encode the artifact, when available. Record the stored format version string if the container supports one.

epoch_extraction.reasoning: For the epoch_extraction Process node, I included only the transformation settings for extracting stimulus-locked EEG windows: epoch window bounds, baseline correction choices, event alignment rules, trial rejection strategy, and output quality indicators. I excluded the cleaned EEG artifact properties because those belong to clean_eeg_signal, and I excluded the resulting epoch dataset properties because those belong to eeg_epochs. I also avoided any capture hardware or stimulus-content descriptors, since this node only describes how windows are cut from the cleaned signal using the timing protocol. No already_generated list was provided, but I kept the schema distinct from earlier process and signal nodes to avoid semantic overlap.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or library used to extract stimulus-locked EEG epochs from the cleaned signal. Example: 'MNE-Python', 'EEGLAB', or another epoching package.
Version of the epoching software used during stimulus-locked window extraction. Record the exact version string active when the epoch extraction step was run.
Start time in milliseconds relative to the alignment event used to define each epoch window. Typical ERP windows begin before stimulus onset, for example -200 ms.
End time in milliseconds relative to the alignment event used to define each epoch window. Typical ERP windows extend several hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset.

Start time in milliseconds for the baseline correction interval relative to the alignment event, if baseline correction is applied. Record the nominal pre-event baseline window used during epoch extraction.
End time in milliseconds for the baseline correction interval relative to the alignment event, if baseline correction is applied. This usually marks the time immediately before stimulus onset.
Type of event used to align epochs, such as stimulus onset, cue onset, or response onset. Record the event reference that anchors the extracted windows.
Code or label filter used to select which events were epoch-locked, recorded as the protocol-defined event selection rule. Store the selection criterion as a flat string if needed.
Method used to reject invalid epochs during extraction, such as peak-to-peak thresholding, artifact annotation, or manual exclusion.
Amplitude threshold in microvolts used to reject epochs during extraction, if threshold-based rejection was applied. Record the cutoff used on the cleaned EEG.

Minimum number of accepted epochs required per condition or subject for the extraction to be considered usable, if such a criterion is defined. Record the study’s quality threshold as an integer count.
Overall technical quality indicator for the extracted epochs, such as whether the windowing and rejection produced analysis-ready data. Record the process outcome at the end of extraction.

eeg_epochs.reasoning: For the eeg_epochs Derivative node, I included only the properties of the extracted epoch dataset itself: dataset identity, number of epochs/trials, channel and time dimensions, epoch window bounds as stored, condition grouping, storage location, and dataset-level completeness/quality. I excluded the epoching procedure and rejection rules because those belong to epoch_extraction, and I excluded raw or cleaned continuous-signal properties because those belong to the signal nodes. I also avoided stimulus-content details and ERP summaries, which are owned by upstream stimulus/response derivatives and downstream ERP derivation. This schema is focused on the reusable epoch dataset as a computed artifact.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the EEG epochs dataset after stimulus-locked extraction. Use a stable string such as 'sub-001_epochs'.
Technical storage format of the epochs dataset, recorded for the computed epoch artifact. Examples include FIF, MAT, HDF5, NWB, or other structured epoch containers.
Total number of accepted EEG epochs contained in the dataset, counted after extraction and rejection. This is the number of trial windows available for analysis.
Number of EEG channels represented in each epoch, counted in the stored epoch dataset. This should reflect the post-extraction data dimensions.
Number of time samples per epoch in the dataset, counted across the stored epoch window. Use the actual epoch length represented in samples.
Start time in milliseconds relative to the alignment event for epochs stored in the dataset. Record the window boundary encoded in the computed artifact.
End time in milliseconds relative to the alignment event for epochs stored in the dataset. Record the window boundary encoded in the computed artifact.
Time unit used for epoch sample indexing or timestamps in the stored dataset, such as milliseconds or seconds. Record the unit encoded in the computed epochs artifact.
Set of condition labels represented in the epochs dataset, corresponding to the trial groups included in the computed artifact. Store the labels as a flat string if needed.
Fraction of extracted epochs retained after rejection, relative to the total candidate epochs. Use a proportion between 0 and 1 as a dataset-level quality indicator.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the epochs dataset is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the computed artifact location.
Technical completeness flag indicating whether the epochs dataset appears intact and fully written after extraction. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the computed artifact.

erp_averaging.reasoning: For the erp_averaging Process node, I included only the averaging operation parameters and output-quality information: software identity, averaging strategy, trial inclusion criteria, weighting, baseline handling at the averaging stage, and summary quality indicators. I excluded the epoch dataset properties because those belong to eeg_epochs, and I excluded the resulting ERP waveform artifact properties because those belong to erp_waveform. I also avoided adding stimulus or response semantics, since this node only describes how condition-wise averages are computed from epochs. No already_generated list was provided here, so I kept the schema unique to the averaging process while respecting upstream/downstream boundaries.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or library used to compute condition-wise ERP averages from EEG epochs. Example: 'MNE-Python', 'EEGLAB', or another averaging package.
Version of the ERP averaging software used to derive event-related potentials. Record the exact version string active when the averaging step was run.
Method used to combine trials into ERP waveforms, such as simple mean, weighted mean, or robust averaging. Record the condition-level averaging rule used in the computation.
Rule used to weight trials during ERP averaging, if weights are applied. Store the study-defined weighting approach as a categorical descriptor.
Minimum number of accepted epochs required within each condition before ERP averaging is performed or considered valid. Record the study-defined trial-count threshold as an integer.
Whether baseline correction is applied at the averaging stage when computing ERP waveforms. Record this as a process-level flag for the averaging operation.
Baseline interval in milliseconds used for ERP averaging or re-baselining, if applicable. Record the nominal pre-event interval used in the averaging procedure.
Scope at which epochs are combined during averaging, such as per condition, per subject, or per block. For ERP derivation this is usually condition-level.
Policy governing whether epochs are excluded from averaging based on prior quality flags or rejection annotations. Record the inclusion rule used before computing the ERP.
Overall quality indicator for the resulting averaged ERP computation, such as whether waveforms have sufficient signal-to-noise for interpretation. Record this at the end of the averaging step.

erp_waveform.reasoning: For the erp_waveform Derivative node, I included only properties of the computed ERP artifact itself: waveform identity, storage format, dimensions, time axis, channel/condition structure, and derived quality metrics such as number of averages contributing and signal-to-noise indicators. I excluded the averaging procedure, trial inclusion logic, and baseline correction settings because those belong to erp_averaging. I also excluded raw epoch properties and stimulus/response metadata because those are upstream or separate nodes. No already_generated list was provided, so I kept the schema strictly artifact-centered and avoided repeating fields that would semantically belong to earlier process or signal nodes.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the ERP waveform artifact computed from averaged EEG epochs. Use a stable string such as 'sub-001_erp'.
Technical storage format of the ERP waveform artifact, recorded for the computed time course. Examples include FIF, MAT, HDF5, NWB, or other ERP container formats.
Number of EEG channels represented in the ERP waveform artifact, counted in the stored computed output. This reflects the dimensionality of the ERP data.
Number of conditions represented in the ERP waveform artifact, counted in the computed output. Record how many condition-specific averages are stored.
Number of time points in each ERP waveform, counted across the stored averaged time course. Use the sample count encoded in the artifact.
Start time in milliseconds of the ERP time course relative to the alignment event, as stored in the computed artifact. This typically includes a pre-stimulus baseline interval.
End time in milliseconds of the ERP time course relative to the alignment event, as stored in the computed artifact. Record the full analysis window encoded in the waveform.
Time unit used for the ERP waveform axis, such as milliseconds or seconds. Record the unit encoded in the stored ERP artifact.
Number of epochs contributing to each condition-specific ERP average, recorded as a dataset-level summary or stored as a representative count if uniform. Use the post-averaging contribution count.
Signal-to-noise ratio or comparable quality metric for the ERP waveform, measured on the computed artifact. Record the dataset-level ERP quality indicator if available.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the ERP waveform is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the computed artifact location.

Technical completeness flag indicating whether the ERP waveform file or object appears intact and fully written after computation. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the ERP artifact.

behavioral_summary.reasoning: For the behavioral_summary Process node, I included only the transformation settings and summary definitions used to aggregate raw responses by condition: software identity, summarization method, reaction-time trimming rules, accuracy definitions, aggregation scope, and output-quality indicators. I excluded the raw response artifact properties because those belong to response_signal, and I excluded the resulting summary artifact properties because those belong to response_summary. I also avoided EEG/ERP-specific fields and stimulus-timing details because this node only describes how behavioral measures are computed from response data for later joint analysis. No already_generated list was provided, so I kept the schema process-specific and non-overlapping with upstream/downstream nodes.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or library used to summarize behavioral responses by condition. Example: 'Python', 'Pandas', or another analysis package used for response summarization.
Version of the software used to compute behavioral summaries. Record the exact version string active when the summarization step was run.
Repository or distribution source for the summarization software, if relevant to reproducibility. Use a stable URL or package source string when available.
Method used to aggregate reaction times and choices by stimulus condition, such as mean, median, proportion correct, or robust summary. Record the analysis rule applied to raw responses.
Rule used to trim or exclude implausible reaction times before summarization, if applied. Record the study-defined lower/upper bounds or exclusion policy as a flat string.
Definition used to score response accuracy during behavioral summarization, such as match-to-target, correct-choice, or task-specific criterion. Record the scoring rule applied to raw choices.
Unit at which behavioral responses are aggregated, such as per condition, per subject, per block, or per session. For this workflow the summaries are typically condition-level.
Minimum number of valid responses required within a condition or subject before a summary is produced or considered valid. Record the study-defined count threshold as an integer.
Policy for handling missing, late, or invalid responses during summarization, such as exclusion, imputation, or separate coding. Record the behavioral summary rule used for incomplete data.
Overall quality indicator for the summarized behavioral outputs, such as whether the summary is suitable for downstream joint analysis. Record the process outcome at the end of summarization.

response_summary.reasoning: For the response_summary Derivative node, I included only the properties of the computed behavioral summary artifact itself: its name, storage format, table dimensions, condition and subject grouping, summary metric set, value units, and storage/completeness indicators. I excluded the summarization method, trimming rules, and accuracy definition because those belong to the behavioral_summary Process node. I also excluded raw response-event properties because those belong to response_signal. This keeps the schema centered on the reusable summarized behavioral dataset that will be joined with ERP outputs in the downstream analysis.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the summarized behavioral response artifact. Use a stable string such as 'sub-001_response_summary'.
Technical storage format of the behavioral summary artifact, recorded for the computed table or file. Examples include CSV, TSV, JSON, HDF5, or other summary formats.
Number of rows or records in the behavioral summary table, counted after aggregation by condition or subject. Use the stored artifact dimension as the row count.
Number of columns or variables in the behavioral summary table, counted in the stored artifact. This reflects the dimensionality of the summarized behavioral data.
Grouping level represented in the summary artifact, such as per subject, per session, or per cohort. Record the unit at which behavioral measures are stored in the summarized output.
Condition grouping used in the summary artifact, indicating how response measures are stratified by experimental condition. Store the condition label structure encoded in the summary.
Set of behavioral metrics included in the summarized response artifact, such as accuracy, reaction time, or omission rate. Store the metric names as a flat string if needed.
Unit used for reaction time values in the summary artifact, typically milliseconds. Record the unit used for the summarized latency measures.
Type of accuracy metric stored in the summary artifact, such as proportion correct or percentage correct. Record the summary-level accuracy representation used downstream.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the behavioral summary is stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the summarized artifact location.

Technical completeness flag indicating whether the behavioral summary file or table appears intact and fully written after computation. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the summary artifact.

joint_erp_analysis.reasoning: For the joint_erp_analysis Process node, I included only the analysis-operation metadata that describes how ERP features are combined with stimulus-condition and behavioral-summary inputs: analysis software identity, statistical/modeling approach, feature-selection rules, covariate handling, multiple-comparison correction, and output-quality indicators. I excluded the source ERP waveform, response summary, and stimulus protocol properties because those belong to upstream nodes. I also excluded the final analysis outputs because those belong to erp_analysis_results. No already_generated list was provided, but I still avoided duplicating fields that would semantically overlap with earlier process or derivative nodes, especially stimulus_count/condition_count-style fields that have already been used elsewhere. The schema is focused on reproducible joint-analysis settings rather than the data being analyzed or the final results.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or library used to perform the joint ERP analysis. Example: 'Python', 'MNE-Python', 'statsmodels', or another analysis environment.
Version of the analysis software used for the joint ERP and behavior analysis. Record the exact version string active when the analysis step was run.
Repository or distribution source for the analysis software, if relevant to reproducibility. Use a stable URL, package source, or commit reference when available.

Type of statistical or computational model used to relate ERP features to stimulus conditions and behavioral summaries, such as regression, mixed-effects model, or classification. Record the primary joint-analysis approach.
Set of ERP features entered into the joint analysis, such as mean amplitude, peak latency, area under the curve, or component-specific measures. Store the feature names as a flat string if needed.
Set of behavioral summary features included in the joint analysis, such as accuracy, reaction time, or omission rate. Store the feature names as a flat string if needed.
Additional covariates included in the joint analysis, such as subject age, condition order, or trial count. Store the covariate names as a flat string if needed.
Correction method applied for multiple statistical tests in the joint ERP analysis, if any. Record the study-defined correction approach used for inference.
Nominal significance threshold used for the joint analysis, usually expressed as a proportion such as 0.05. Record the inference threshold applied to the statistical tests.
Effect size metric reported or computed in the joint analysis, such as beta coefficient, Cohen's d, partial eta squared, or odds ratio. Record the primary effect-size descriptor used.
Overall quality indicator for the joint ERP analysis, such as whether the model fit and inputs were suitable for interpretation. Record the process outcome at the end of the analysis step.

erp_analysis_results.reasoning: For the erp_analysis_results Derivative node, I included only the final computed-result properties: result artifact identity, format, dimensions, storage location, and high-level statistical outcome summaries. I excluded analysis procedures, model choice, and correction settings because those belong to the joint_erp_analysis Process node. I also excluded upstream ERP waveform and behavioral-summary properties because those are inputs, not the final result artifact. The schema is therefore focused on the reusable endpoint output of the workflow, capturing what a downstream user needs to locate, inspect, and interpret the final analysis deliverable.

md_schema.descr: Name or identifier for the final ERP analysis result artifact. Use a stable string such as 'sub-001_erp_analysis_results'.
Technical storage format of the final ERP analysis output, recorded for the computed result artifact. Examples include CSV, TSV, JSON, HDF5, NWB, or other results formats.
Number of rows or result records in the final analysis output table, counted after the joint ERP analysis has been completed. Use the stored artifact dimension as the row count.
Number of columns or variables in the final analysis output table, counted in the stored result artifact. This reflects the dimensionality of the analysis output.

Primary scientific target of the final analysis output, describing what the results relate to in this workflow. For this DAG the target should connect ERPs with visual stimulus conditions and subject responses.
Whether the result artifact includes statistical summaries such as p-values, effect sizes, or model coefficients. Record this as a final-output feature flag.
Number of statistically significant effects reported in the final results, if the artifact includes inferential summaries. Record the count as reported in the computed output.
Primary outcome metric summarized in the final analysis results, such as ERP amplitude, latency, accuracy association, or reaction time association. Record the main endpoint reported by the analysis.
File system path, object store URI, or database location where the final analysis results are stored. Use a resolvable string identifier for the result artifact location.

Technical completeness flag indicating whether the final analysis result file or table appears intact and fully written after computation. Record this as a storage-level quality indicator for the result artifact.
